caption: Different expressions can identify the same person.

narration.text: Lewis Carroll. Charles Dodgson. The mathematician. The author of Alice.
Different expressions, but in the right context, they can all refer to the same person. An identity can outlast a name.

caption: A name is one way into a passage.

narration.text: Name-based linking is a useful way to connect documents and ideas. But natural language rarely refers to someone by the same name every time.
What if we could make those connections without changing the way we write?

caption: Earlier mentions give a name a history.

narration.text: An entity may have a name and several aliases. Here, the pen name and the full personal name lead to the same person.
But a phrase like the mathematician can lead there too, because a reader used it in an earlier annotation.
Each new mention can add another route to that person. The phrase still belongs to its particular passage.

caption: Hold the target. Vary the search.

narration.text: The words we select need not be the words we search for. Here, the selected words are the mathematician.
Watch the highlight as we try Dodgson, the full personal name, and finally Lewis Carroll. Only the search changes.
When we choose the person, the connection lands on the words we originally selected.

caption: One judgement can connect several passages.

narration.text: Now take a longer document. Dodgson appears in four different paragraphs. We begin by selecting just one occurrence.
With the person prepared, we can review the other occurrences of the same expression throughout this document.
Each highlighted range is a proposed target. Read them in context before deciding which to include.
One binding operation now creates four separate mentions. The text stays where it was.
Carroll, the author. Carroll, a neighbour who stopped by with a letter. The words match.
The people are different. It is the author who decides which connections to make.

caption: Two ways to write an entity mention.

narration.text: We can also make a connection as we write. Square brackets open an entity search. Choose Lewis Carroll, and his name completes the phrase.
Parentheses make a different choice possible. Type the author of Alice, then search independently for the person you mean.
Accept the result, and those exact words stay in the sentence. Both gestures leave a mention pointing to the same person.

caption: Earlier language opens a new route to the person.

narration.text: Suppose we have also linked the phrase the Oxford lecturer. Once that document is saved and indexed, its wording can help us elsewhere.
In a new document, search previous mentions for that phrase. We can use yesterday’s words to identify the person in today’s writing.
We need not choose between the richness of natural language and the precision of semantic connections.
Our words can remain our own, while the things they refer to become part of a shared structure of knowledge.
Write naturally. Connect semantically.
